workouts.title: What is Strength?
workouts.description: In this course, we'll delve into the concept of strength, which is essentially the capacity to generate force. We'll explore two distinct forms of strength: Relative and Absolute. Relative Strength pertains to the ability to generate force or move loads in proportion to one's body weight. On the other hand, Absolute Strength refers to the sheer amount of force one can generate or the load one can handle regardless of body weight.

workouts.title: What is Periodization?
workouts.description: Coach CJ and Joe break down the 4 variables to periodization (Volume, Frequency, Intensity, Variation) and how they are used in training.

workouts.title: Types of Strength Training
workouts.description: Coach CJ and Coach Joe dissect various types of periodization employed in strength training. Those include but are not limited to: linear periodization, non-linear (or undulating) periodization, concurrent training (aka CrossFit), block periodization and emerging periodization. They also delve into why RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion) works effectively with the Raw Strength programming and how this course employs different periodization types throughout its design.

workouts.title: Strength Adaptation
workouts.description: Strength adaptations encompass both physical and non-physical transformations that occur within the body during training. In this video, Coach CJ and Coach Joe elaborate on those changes, providing a range of examples and explanations.

workouts.title: Recovery & Growth
workouts.description: Coach CJ and Coach Joe delve into the topics of fatigue and recovery, explaining how these factors are managed within the framework of the Raw Strength programming.

workouts.title: Specificity
workouts.description: Specificity is king when it comes to strength adaptations and gains. For that reason, this course prioritizes strength-building exercises and recommends minimizing exposure to excessive aerobic and conditioning training to maximize potential strength gains and optimize recovery.

workouts.title: Volume & Progressive Loading
workouts.description: Since the advent of sports science, the prevailing approach to strength training has often emphasized increasing volume and load to prompt the body's adaptation and growth. These concepts are not new; even in late 6th century B.C., the Greek athlete Milo of Croton famously demonstrated progressive overload by lifting a newborn calf each day until it matured into a bull he could carry. However, what we've learned is that specificity and intentionality outweigh volume and load increases over time. While volume and progressive loading remain fundamental in strength training, fixating solely on them risks impeding recovery and growth. Instead we use concepts like RPE and specificity to prioritize training quality and focus.

workouts.title: Variation & Accessory Work
workouts.description: Movement variation involves modifying specific movements to adjust their load or impact on the body, while still promoting the transfer of strength and/or skill to the primary movement. For instance, using variations like banded strict press, paused strict press, or seated Z press can enhance the strict press. Although each movement differs from the strict press itself, it remains within the same movement spectrum, contributing to progress with the primary movement. Similarly, accessory work, which may include but not limited to movement variations, is typically performed towards the end of workouts. This approach allows us to continue training under fatigue, utilizing a range of movements that further support and advance our primary training goals.

workouts.title: Hitting Plateaus
workouts.description: Hitting plateaus is a common occurrence in training and signifies a point where we're no longer adapting to training stressors or making measurable progress. As our training age (the duration of our training experience) increases, it becomes increasingly important to employ strategies to offset plateaus. This is where the principles of specificity and variation play crucial roles.

workouts.title: [Please Read] What is RPE? ⚠️
workouts.description: In this overview of subjective assessments, Coach Joe dissects RPE, RIR, Anchoring, and Proximity to Failure, explaining how to integrate these concepts effectively within the Raw Strength programming. Additionally, research indicates that training to failure (RPE 9-10) isn't necessary to achieve optimal results. So, you'll note that the Raw Strength programming often incorporates training ranges of 6-8 RPE to maximize benefits while minimizing negative outcomes. If you feel you need more familiarity with RPE, we've included an optional Anchoring Week to provide additional exposure to RPE scales before progressing to Week 9 of the programming. Remember RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion) and RIR (Reps In Reserve) is all based on how you feel in the moment. So, if you managed 10 reps at RPE 8 yesterday, that might change the next day if you're fatigued and can only do, say, 5 reps.

sections.name: TERMS

items.movement: RIR (Reps in Reserve) - Another subjective assessment that enables you to determine, in real-time, how many reps you have left before reaching total failure. To make it easy, with raw Strength we essentially combine RIR into RPE.
Anchoring - Calibrating your RPE scale by taking a set to failure and aligning your initial perception of effort (RPE rating) with the actual intensity level on the RPE scale.
Proximity to Failure - indicates how close you are to reaching muscular failure during an exercise. It relates to both Reps in Reserve (RIR) and Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE).

sections.format: RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion) - A subjective rating out of 10 that assesses the perceived difficulty of the current exercise and provides actionable context on your performance.

workouts.title: The Valsalva Maneuver
workouts.description: The Valsalva Maneuver focuses on creating internal pressure and mid-line stability by bracing against a closed glottis (aka closed lungs). This bracing technique resembles tensing your core as if preparing to withstand a punch to the stomach. To perform the Valsalva Maneuver, simply take a deep breath, hold it by pushing the air outward, then execute the lift. Exhale once the lift is complete. Using a weightlifting belt can enhance this technique by providing something to push against, or a tactile input.

workouts.title: Strength for Sport
workouts.description: Coach CJ discusses the significance of strength and the six focused lifts in Raw Strength within the context of CrossFit. He explains how developing various aspects of strength, such as strength under fatigue, speed strength, and strength endurance, can enhance not only CrossFit performance and General Physical Preparedness (GPP), but also improve gymnastic skills and shapes. In essence, the stronger you become, the more well-rounded CrossFit athlete you can be.

workouts.title: Food Fuels Gains
workouts.description: Food is essential for fueling gains. Whether your goal is to be in a caloric surplus or deficit, it's crucial to aim for at least one gram of protein per pound of body weight to support strength gains and muscle repair. Additionally, if you experience fatigue during training, consider increasing your carbohydrate intake.

workouts.title: Mental Resilience for Lifting
workouts.description: Coach Ben, CJ, and Joe dive into the importance of mindset and setting realistic expectations. Emphasizing the significance of being intentional and giving your best effort each day. They also highlight the value of enjoying the process and embracing the 'Do Hard Things' mantra. Interested in guided mental strength training? Check out WODprep's 30-day mental strength course, Strong Mind. WODprep Academy athletes can find it in their WODprep library, while WODprep athletes automatically save 50% by following this link.

workouts.title: Strength & Lifting Gear
workouts.description: Coach CJ and Joe explore the various gear options for strength training, including knee sleeves, wrist wraps, wrist straps, weightlifting belts, shoes, and thumb tape, discussing when and how each should be used. It's important to note that gear should not be used as a a band-aid solution or a tool to alleviate pain. Nor should it compensate for any weaknesses in strength. Instead, gear should be seen as a tool to enhance your current strength levels, especially as you approach maximal lifts. It should not be necessary during lower-intensity training sessions.

workouts.title: Bench Press Fault Fixer
workouts.description: Here are the top 3 fault fixers categories for the Bench Press: Ensure the feet are flat on the floor, connected firmly, and positioned under the knees to maintain optimal leg drive. With the bench press teaching in mind, we want to make sure we are not too low (into the belly) OR to high (into the neck) when we lower the bar to our sternum. Guide the bar in a J-like trajectory, starting over the shoulders and moving toward the sternum or top of the rib cage at the bottom position. From a side profile the bar will look like it is coming lower on your body from the start position (that is good). We do not want it to come straight down into your neck. As you press it back up it will shift over your shoulders and be directly above your shoulders at lockout.

workouts.title: Deadlift Fault Fixer
workouts.description: Here are the most common deadlift faults. Avoid wearing thick sole shoes or olympic lifters when performing the deadlift. Deadlift physics get wonky as the bar gets to close or too far from the body. If the set-up becomes too upright, it becomes more quad dominant and adds unnecessary movement to the deadlift. Hips move before shoulders and places additional demands on the hamstrings. Focus on keeping the lower back neutral . Some people overextending the back and lean back thinking it's a proper lockout. It isn't. Avoid sitting the weight on the knees which makes the last half of the deadlift more difficult. Avoid hitting your knees by simply performing the same steps of the deadlift in reverse as you bring it down.

workouts.title: Front Squat Fault Fixer
workouts.description: Here are the most common Front Squat faults and the cues to assist you in overcoming them. Strive to maintain high elbows (rather than allowing them to drop) to establish a stable front rack position, allowing the bar to rest just above the collarbone. You may need to loosen your grip and hold the bar with your fingers to achieve the required range to elevate the elbows Many athletes adopt back squat mechanics by pushing their hips back when starting the squat. However, this can pose challenges in maintaining an upright chest and a proper front rack position in the Front Squat. If you find yourself in this situation, start the front squat with the knees moving forward, enabling the hips to drop straight down instead of backward. If you feel like you're being 'pancaked' in the bottom of the squat, concentrate on staying tight and stiff in your back. Athletes often relax their back as they descend, making it difficult to hold a front rack position and placing excessive stress on the wrists and back.

workouts.title: Back Squat Fault Fixer
workouts.description: Here are the most common faults when it comes to the back Squat and how to fix them. When athletes strive to maintain an upright torso and keep their elbows back, they often end up leading with their knees, which shifts their center of gravity forward instead of back. To correct this, focus on pushing the hips back to initiate the squat and keeping the full foot in contact with the floor. The movement standard in CrossFit and powerlifting is to descend so the hips go below the top of the knee. For athletes aiming to compete in these sports, ensuring you develop and can reach correct depth is crucial. As we come up from the bottom of the squat, the aim is to preserve our back angle and avoid prematurely shooting the hips upward. Doing so can cause the back squat to resemble a Good Morning or Kang Squat, leading to unnecessary strain on the lower back.

workouts.title: Strict Press Fault Fixer
workouts.description: Here are the top faults when performing the Strict Press: It's crucial to keep the quads and glutes tight to maximize the upward force applied to the bar. If we're too loose in any of these areas, our potential force output is diminished. Moving the bar out-and-away from your body reduces the load you can effectively move. Ensure the bar travels as vertically as possible by pulling the head back to facilitate the ideal bar path. If your top position feels locked or resembles a chicken wing with the elbows out focus on keeping everything facing forward to counter and keep you in a ideal position. Unlike the front squat, we don't want to keep the elbows high in the set-up position. Instead we want the elbows down to maximize vertical pressing force and avoid getting caught in an out-and-away bar path.

workouts.title: Pendlay Row Fault Fixer
workouts.description: Here a some of the most common faults of the Pendlay Row so you can work through them if your experiencing them. Watch your grip doesn't go too wide. Aim for a grip just outside the shoulders. Keep the back tight with the arms long so there is no rounding. The Pendlay Row is primarily a stationary movement. As the load increases, avoid throwing the shoulders back in an attempt to create momentum to move the weight. Instead, it should be a static pull from the floor to the chest. If you're having difficulty getting the bar to the chest cleanly, consider using a lighter weight.

workouts.description: Test Week serves as the foundation, establishing a baseline from which we'll measure your progress over the next 9 weeks of strength training. This assessment will help us identify the two lifts that need the most attention so, we can focus on their development. During Test Week, aim to schedule your testing days on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday to ensure ample recovery between each session. If that’s not possible, allow for at least one full day of rest after two consecutive days of lifting. Additionally, you can print out the Test Week lift sheet under the FILES tab.

workouts.title: Anchor Week Overview
workouts.description: This optional week is designed to enhance your understanding of RPE, particularly if it's a new concept for you, and more importantly, how to incorporate it throughout the Raw Strength programming. First, let's revisit RPE to ensure we're all on the same page. Take a look at this chart and observe how the RPE (highlighted in red boxes) corresponds to the intensity of the working set. During Anchor Week, we'll assess your RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion) accuracy. Aim to schedule your anchor days on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday to ensure ample recovery between each session. If that’s not possible, allow for at least one full day of rest after two consecutive days of lifting. Here's how it works: We'll take a weight you previously lifted for a certain number of reps and compare it to the RPE rating you gave that set. For example, if you lifted 200lbs for a single back squat and rated it as RPE 8, according to the RPE chart, you should have been able to do 2 more repetitions with that weight before reaching failure. So, in Anchor Week, we'll push you to failure with a certain weight to determine how many repetitions you can complete. If you exceed expectations, it indicates you overrated the RPE; if you fall short, you underrated it. This process will give you a better understanding and feel for RPE. If you achieved over 7 repetitions on your max reps, it suggests you're capable of lifting more weight than you initially thought and are overrating your RPE. So, what you perceived as an 8 was likely closer to a 7 or even a 6 if you managed significantly more reps. Conversely, if you completed fewer than 7 repetitions, it indicates you've been underrating your RPE, meaning the lifts were more challenging than you perceived. In this case, your initial set might have been closer to an 8.5-9.5. To achieve a true RPE of 8, you would reduce the weight on the bar.
